body.text: Form follows physics in Electric car, where structural load, light, and material permanence meet human experience. Look closely at the spatial geometry and you see how design endures across decades.
An electric car is an automobile that uses electrical energy as the primary source of propulsion.

The term normally refers to a plug-in electric vehicle, typically a battery electric vehicle (BEV), which only uses energy stored in on-board battery packs, but broadly may also include plug-in hybrid electric vehicle (PHEV), range-extended electric vehicle (REEV) and fuel cell electric vehicle (FCEV), which can convert electric power from other fuels via a generator or a fuel cell.
Compared to conventional internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles, electric cars are quieter, more responsive, have superior energy conversion efficiency and produce no tailpipe emissions.

Electric cars generally have a lower overall carbon footprint over their life cycle, from manufacturing to end of life, even when the electricity used for charging comes partly from fossil-fuel power stations. Electric cars generally have higher manufacturing emissions than comparable ICE vehicles, although they produce fewer greenhouse gas emissions during operation.

Due to the superior efficiency of electric motors, electric cars also generate less waste heat, thus reducing the need for engine cooling systems that are often large, complicated and maintenance-prone in ICE vehicles. However, EVs may still use dedicated thermal management systems to regulate battery temperature.

The battery of a plug-in electric car is typically recharged by connecting it to an external electricity supply. Recharging an electric car can be done at different kinds of charging stations, depending on local regulations and utility requirements, these charging stations can be installed in private homes, parking garages and public areas.

There is also research and development in, as well as deployment of, other technologies such as battery swapping and inductive charging. As charging stations (especially fast chargers) become more widely available, range anxiety and the time required to charge remain psychological barriers for some consumers considering the purchase of an electric car.
Governments and electric vehicle manufacturers have introduced various initiatives to expand charging infrastructure, improve charging accessibility and address these concerns.
Worldwide, 21 million plug-in electric cars were sold in 2025, accounting for one-quarter of new car sales and representing an increase of more than 20% compared with 2024.

Many countries have established government incentives for plug-in electric vehicles, including tax credits, subsidies, and other non-monetary incentives while several countries have legislated to phase-out of fossil fuel vehicles, to reduce air pollution and limit climate change.

As of 2020, the total cost of ownership of recent electric vehicles in the United States and European Union was lower than that of equivalent ICE cars, due to lower power and maintenance costs.

In 2023, the Tesla Model Y became the world's best-selling car. The Tesla Model 3 became the world's all-time best-selling electric car in early 2020, and in June 2021 it became the first electric car to pass 1 million global sales.
Terminology

The term "electric car" typically refers specifically to battery electric vehicles (BEVs) or all-electric cars, a type of electric vehicle (EV) that has an onboard rechargeable battery pack that can be plugged in and charged from the electric grid, or at home with solar panels, and the electricity stored on the vehicle is the only energy source that provides propulsion for the wheels.

The term generally refers to highway-capable automobiles, but there are also low-speed electric vehicles with limitations in terms of weight, power, and maximum speed that are allowed to travel on certain public roads. The latter are classified as Neighborhood Electric Vehicles (NEVs) in the United States, and as electric motorised quadricycles in Europe.
History
Early developments
Between 1832 and 1839, the Scottish inventor Robert Anderson developed a crude electric carriage.
In 1881, Gustave Trouvé presented an electric car driven by an improved Siemens motor at the Exposition internationale d'Électricité de Paris.
In 1882 Werner von Siemens presented the Electromote, the world's first trolleybus, in Berlin.

In 1884, Thomas Parker built an electric car in Wolverhampton, England, using his own specially designed high-capacity rechargeable batteries, although the only documentation is a photograph from 1895.
In 1888, the German inventor Andreas Flocken designed the Flocken Elektrowagen, regarded as the first "real" electric car.
In 1890, William Morrison introduced the first practical electric car to the United States.

Electricity was among the preferred methods for automobile propulsion in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, providing a level of comfort and an ease of operation that could not be achieved by the era's internal combustion cars. The electric vehicle fleet then peaked at approximately 30,000 vehicles.

In 1897, electric cars found commercial use as taxis in Britain and in the United States. In London, Bersey electric cabs were the first self-propelled vehicles for hire at a time when cabs were horse-drawn.

In 1897, New York City had a fleet of twelve hansom cabs and one brougham, based on the Electrobat II, introduced as part of a project partly funded by the Philadelphia Electric Storage Battery Company.

During the 20th century, the main US manufacturers of electric vehicles included Anthony Electric, Baker, Columbia, Anderson, Edison, Riker, Milburn Wagon Company (Milburn Light Electric), Bailey Electric, and Detroit Electric.
Six electric cars held the land speed record in the 19th century.

Electric cars remained popular until advances in internal-combustion engine (ICE) cars left them behind. At the time, the shorter refueling times and lower production costs of ICE vehicles made them more attractive to consumers than electric cars.
A decisive moment came with the 1912 introduction of the electric starter motor that replaced laborious and dangerous methods such as hand-cranking.
Renaissance

In the early 1990s the California Air Resources Board began to push for lower-emissions vehicles, with the ultimate goal of zero-emissions vehicles. Automakers responded with electric models, although they were later withdrawn.

California electric-automaker Tesla Motors began development in 2004 of what became the Tesla Roadster, first delivered to customers in 2008. The Roadster was the first highway-legal all-electric car to use lithium-ion battery cells, and the first production all-electric car to travel more than 320 km (200 miles) per charge.
Better Place developed battery charging and battery swapping services, but went bankrupt in 2013.

The 2009 Mitsubishi i-MiEV was the first highway-legal series production electric car, and the first to sell more than 10,000 units. The Nissan Leaf, launched in 2010, quickly surpassed it as the best-selling all-electric car.

In 2008, advances in battery technology, and the desire to reduce Greenhouse gas emissions and improve urban air quality increased interest in EVs. During the 2010s, EVs in China expanded rapidly with government support.

In July 2019 Motor Trend awarded the Tesla Model S the title "ultimate car of the year". In March 2020 the Tesla Model 3 passed the Nissan Leaf to become the best-selling electric car, with more than 500,000 units delivered, it reached 1 million units in June 2021.
In 2021, the Alliance for Automotive Innovation reported that the 187,000 sales of electric vehicles accounted for 6% of US light-duty vehicles.
Economics
EVs typically have a much lower cost of ownership than ICE vehicles. Early differences in purchase cost have shrunk due to intense competitive pressures.
Total cost of ownership

Generally, electricity costs less than petrol per kilometre travelled, although petrol and electricity prices vary dramatically by location, origin and even time of day. Petrol prices are affected by taxes and fuel formulation, while electricity can come from sources such as rooftop solar or the electric grid.
EV motors are far more efficient than internal combustion engines, which convert at least 60% of the energy they consume into heat rather than propulsion.
The greater the distance driven per year, the more likely the total cost of ownership for an EV is less than for an equivalent ICE car.
EV drivers can save approximately 50% on maintenance and repair costs because EVs have a simpler mechanical structure and fewer moving parts than ICE vehicles.
